**Video:** [Lec 51 — Positional Embeddings](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xbkJIeLoGyw)

## Learning goals

- See why bag-of-tokens attention is **permutation-equivariant** without positions.
- Write the **sinusoidal** positional encoding from Vaswani et al.
- Contrast fixed sinusoids with **learned** absolute position embeddings (and note relative variants).

## Before this clicks

Self-attention mixes tokens by content. If you shuffle the input embeddings, the set of pairwise scores is the same up to permutation — the model does not “know” order from attention alone. RNNs baked order into time steps; Transformers add **positional signals** to embeddings so $e_i$ and $e_j$ differ when $i\neq j$ even if the tokens match.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Inject position into the residual stream

Common absolute scheme: add a position vector $p_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ to the token embedding $t_i$:

$$
e_i = t_i + p_i.
$$

Then every later layer sees content **and** location.

### 2. Sinusoidal positional encoding

For dimension index $k=0,\ldots,d/2-1$ and position $i$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_i^{(2k)} &= \sin\!\left(\frac{i}{10000^{2k/d}}\right),\\
p_i^{(2k+1)} &= \cos\!\left(\frac{i}{10000^{2k/d}}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Even dims: sine; odd dims: cosine; wavelengths stretch geometrically across channels. No parameters — same formula for any length (extrapolation is imperfect but defined).

**Intuition:** different frequencies give a unique “fingerprint” for each $i$; linear functions of $p_i$ can represent relative offsets $i-j$ in useful ways (paper’s motivation).

### 3. Learned absolute embeddings

Store a table $P\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{\max}\times d}$ and set $p_i=P_i$ for $i<L_{\max}$. Trained with the rest of the model. Simple and strong inside the training length; weaker if you need $i>L_{\max}$ unless you extend carefully.

### 4. Relative and modern variants (awareness)

Many later models encode **relative** distances (how far $j$ is from $i$) inside attention logits, or use rotary embeddings (RoPE), ALiBi, etc. Same problem — order — different parameterization. For this course, absolute sinusoidal vs learned tables are the core contrast.

### 5. Where they sit in the architecture

Positions are added **once** at the bottom (classic Transformer) or sometimes also at other depths; they are not an alternative to multi-head attention — they complement it.

---

## Worked mini-example

$d=4$, position $i=0$: all sines/cosines of $0$ give $p_0=(0,1,0,1)$ (sin $0$, cos $0$, sin $0$, cos $0$). Position $i=1$ yields nonzero sines on even channels and $\cos(\cdot)$ on odd channels — a different vector. Token “cat” at index $0$ vs index $5$ therefore enters attention as two different $e_i$ even if $t_i$ matches.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Attention already knows order | Without $p_i$ (or relative bias), pure content attention is order-blind up to permutation. |
| Sinusoids are learned | In the original paper they are **fixed** formulas. |
| Learned positions work for any length | Table size caps $L_{\max}$ unless you extrapolate. |
| Position replaces token embedding | They are **added** (or otherwise fused), not swapped. |
